transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... honestly, it's just getting to be too much to handle on my own. I came in today because I feel like... well, like I just cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It’s the most frustrating, uncomfortable feeling. You know, at my age, people always tell you that you’re supposed to be slowing down, taking it easy, especially since I'm not working these days and I have the time to just relax. You're supposed to enjoy the quiet. But I just can't do it. 

I'll try to sit down in my chair in the living room, maybe just to rest my legs for a minute or watch a program, and before I even get properly settled, it’s like... it’s like I have to jump up and do the next thing. I'll just suddenly be on my feet again. And half the time I might not even know what that next thing is right away, I just know I absolutely cannot stay in that chair. I'll start wiping down the kitchen counters or rearranging things in the hall closet, just anything to be moving. 

And the thing is... the really hard part about all of this is that I am just so worn out. I am bone-tired most days, and I know I should be sitting still. My body needs me to sit still and just rest. But this feeling inside my skin, it just won't let me. It’s like being a wind-up toy that somebody overwound, and I’m just exhausted from it all, but I can't stop.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

Oh, no, no, it's nothing like that. I mean, I know why you'd ask, because when you're this exhausted all the time and complaining about it, people just assume you must be depressed. My neighbor, Susan, she went through a terrible depression a few years back after her husband passed, and she just sat in the dark all day, wouldn't even open the curtains or answer the phone. But that’s not me at all. I don't feel hopeless, and I certainly haven't lost interest in things. 

If anything, I have too much interest! I still want to do all my hobbies. I love baking, for instance, and I still get so excited looking through my mother's old recipe boxes, planning out what I want to make for the week. I'll get all the ingredients out on the kitchen counter, ready to go. The problem isn't that I don't *want* to do it or that I'm feeling down in the dumps. The problem is just what I was saying before—I can't seem to just settle my body down long enough to actually stand there and mix the batter without feeling that awful urge to go buzz around the house and do something else. 

But my mood? My mood is completely fine, really. I wake up looking forward to the day. I'm not crying or feeling blue or sitting around feeling sorry for myself. I'm just... well, I'm just incredibly frustrated by this whole feeling of being overwound, but I'm definitely not hopeless.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot or feeling anxious about things, even when you know logically there’s no reason to be?

No, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. I mean, everyone worries a little bit, right? Like if my daughter doesn't call when she says she's going to, I might wonder if she got caught in traffic or something, but it's not like I'm sitting there chewing my fingernails off thinking the sky is falling. I don't get that... that pit in my stomach or feel like I can't breathe or anything like that. 

I know some people who are just bundles of nerves, always fretting over every little thing—did I leave the stove on, is the mailman looking at me funny, what if the roof caves in? My sister-in-law is like that, bless her heart. She can't even go to the grocery store without making a list of ten things that could go wrong on the drive there. But me? No, I'm pretty level-headed when it comes to that sort of thing. I don't invent things to panic about. 

It's really just the physical part, you know? That restless, buzzing feeling I was telling you about. It's not my mind racing with worries or fears, it's my body. My mind is perfectly calm, it's just my legs and my hands that want to go, go, go. If I could just get my body to match how calm my mind actually is, I'd be right as rain. So no, no excessive worrying or anxiety here. Just a body that won't listen to reason!
Do you ever feel like you have to keep moving, even when you want to rest, or like you can't stay still no matter how hard you try?

Yes, exactly! That is exactly it. It's like... well, it's like I was saying before, about being that overwound toy, but it's even more than just not being able to sit in my chair. It's my whole day. Most days, I am just going and going and going. I'll start out early, maybe out in the garden—because the weeds, you know, they never stop, and if I don't get out there before the sun gets too hot, it's just miserable. So I'll be out there pulling weeds and deadheading the petunias, and then before I've even put the trowel away, I'm looking at my watch and thinking I need to get over to the senior center. 

I volunteer there on Tuesdays and Thursdays, mostly just helping set up for the activities, maybe pouring coffee. But even when I'm there, I can't just stand behind the coffee urn and chat like the other ladies do. I'm wiping the tables, I'm rearranging the chairs so they're perfectly straight, I'm checking the supply closet to see if we need more napkins. And then, as soon as that's done, I'm off to run errands for the church. Pastor Dave always has a list for me—picking up bulletins from the printer, dropping off a casserole to someone who's sick. I'm happy to do it, I really am, but I do it all at this... this breakneck pace.

And then I finally get home, right? You'd think that would be the time I'd say, "Okay, Margaret, you've done enough today, time to put your feet up." But no. I walk in the door, and immediately I'm looking at the mail on the counter, and I think, "I need to sort those papers right now." So I'm standing there at the kitchen island, sorting bills and junk mail and coupons, not even taking a real breath. It's like... it's like if I stop moving, if I actually sit down and let myself rest, the whole world is just going to fall apart around me. Or at least, that's how my body feels. It's this constant, driving need to be doing something, anything, from the minute I wake up until I finally collapse in bed at night. And even then, sometimes my legs are still twitching! It's just exhausting, doctor, it really is.
Is this feeling of restlessness and needing to move still there even when you're not actively doing tasks, like when you're trying to relax in the evening or fall asleep at night?

Oh, absolutely. That’s the worst part of it, really. You’d think that after running around all day—the garden, the senior center, the errands for Pastor Dave—that my body would just be begging to stop. And my mind is! I want to relax. I really do. But when the evening comes and I try to settle down... well, it’s just impossible. 

I try to do quiet things, things I used to really enjoy. Like, I’ve been working on this Double Wedding Ring quilt pattern for my niece—she’s getting married next June, such a sweet girl, marrying a boy from Columbus—and I try to just sit in my armchair with my sewing hoop. Or I’ll try to sit and read my Bible, maybe do a little devotional before bed. But it never stays quiet for long. I’ll sit there for maybe five minutes, and then I’m humming to myself, or I’m talking out loud about what I need to do tomorrow. Next thing I know, I’m getting up from the chair. I’ll think, "Oh, I just need to go straighten the magazines on the coffee table," or "Let me just go check if the back porch light is off." 

And then I’m just fussing with something else. I’ll be in the kitchen wiping down the counters again, even though I already did it after dinner, or I’ll be reorganizing the tea tins in the pantry. I just can't seem to stay put with my quilting or my reading. The quiet just doesn't last. It’s like the moment I try to be still, that motor inside me just revs up even louder, and I have to get up and do *something*, even if it’s completely unnecessary. It makes the evenings so exhausting because I can’t even enjoy my own downtime!
Have you ever had periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or felt like your thoughts were racing, even if just for a few days?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like I have these... these bursts where I suddenly feel like I could conquer the world or anything like that. And my sleep, well, I need my sleep! If I don't get a good seven or eight hours, I'm just miserable the next day. I mean, my legs might twitch like I told you, but I'm still trying to sleep. I don't feel like I *need* less sleep. I have a friend, Brenda—she's in my Sunday school class—and she went through a phase where she was staying up until three in the morning baking pies and repainting her living room, and she said she felt perfectly fine the next day. I can't even imagine! If I'm up past eleven, I'm practically a zombie the next morning, pouring my coffee into my cereal bowl. 

And as for my thoughts racing, no, it's not my thoughts. Like I was saying before, my mind is actually quite calm. It's my body that's racing. I'm not sitting there having a million brilliant ideas a minute or feeling like my brain is moving faster than my mouth can keep up with. It's just... well, it's just the physical need to be doing things, the fussing and the moving. I don't get these spells where I feel unusually energetic in my mind, just this constant, everyday motor that won't shut off. So no, I haven't had anything like what you're describing, not even for a day or two. Just the same old restless Margaret, day in and day out!
Do you ever feel uncomfortable or agitated if you're not physically active, even if there's no specific task that needs doing?

Oh, yes. Yes, yes, yes. Honestly, doctor, that right there... that is the exact reason I finally made this appointment. That is why I came in. Because I feel like I just cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It’s the most awful, uncomfortable sensation, and it's so hard to explain to anyone else without sounding like a crazy person. 

People look at me and they just think, "Oh, Margaret is such a hard worker, she just loves to keep busy." But it’s not about wanting to be busy at all! It’s that if there isn't a task—if the house is completely spotless, if every single piece of mail is sorted, and there is absolutely nothing that actually needs doing—I still get this terrible, crawling agitation if I try to just *be*. 

I’ll be completely exhausted. I mean, just worn to the bone, my feet aching from standing all day, and I know I should be sitting still. My body desperately needs me to sit still! But I can't do it. I'll be sitting there in my armchair, and my skin just feels so... so tight and uncomfortable, like it's humming or itching from the inside out. And the agitation just builds and builds in my chest until I feel like I absolutely have to jump up and do the next thing. And half the time, there isn't even a 'next thing' to do! I'll just jump up and start pacing the rug, or I'll go wipe down a mirror that's already clean, just to relieve that awful feeling of being trapped in my own resting body. 

It’s just exhausting, being so uncomfortable when you're supposed to be relaxing. Like I said, it’s the whole reason I came in to see you today, because a person at my age really shouldn't feel like they’re trying to jump out of their own skin every time they sit on the sofa, should they?
Is the restlessness you feel mostly in your legs, or does it affect other parts of your body as well?

Well, let me think about that. I know I mentioned my legs earlier, and they certainly do get that twitchy feeling when I try to settle into my armchair. But no, it is definitely not just my legs. It is really my whole self. 

My hands, for instance! If I do not have a dishcloth or my sewing needle or even just a piece of junk mail to fold up and crease, my fingers just do not know what to do with themselves. I will be sitting there and I will start picking at the cuticle on my thumb, which I know is a terrible habit. My mother used to scold me for it when I was a little girl, always telling me to leave my hands alone, but I just cannot help it. They have to be moving.

And then there is that feeling in my chest that I was telling you about, that sort of tight, winding-up sensation. So it is my arms, my hands, my chest... really just an overall buzz. I could not possibly just blame it on my legs. If it were just my legs, maybe I could just tap my foot and be done with it, you know? My husband, God rest his soul, he used to tap his foot when he read the newspaper. Just tap, tap, tap on the floorboards. But he was perfectly relaxed otherwise! 

For me, if I try to just tap my foot to get the energy out, the rest of me starts acting up. My shoulders get tense, I start shifting my weight around, I will be adjusting the throw pillows behind my back five or six times because I just cannot get comfortable. So no, I would not say it is just the legs at all. It is like every inch of me is just waiting for the starting gun to go off, even when I am just trying to watch the evening news!
Do you feel this restlessness even during the day when you're not trying to sit still or relax, like when you're actively doing something?

Well, that's the thing of it, doctor. Yes, yes I do. It's not just when I'm trying to relax, it's... it's all the time. It's like I'm on a treadmill that someone else turned on and forgot to turn off. 

Most days, I am just going from the moment my feet hit the floor. I'll start out in the garden—and you know, a garden takes a lot of work, especially this time of year with the weeds coming up faster than you can pull them—and then I'll rush off to the senior center because they need help setting up for the luncheon, and from there I'm running errands for the church committee. I'm on the altar guild, you see, and there's always something that needs picking up or dropping off. And then I come home, and instead of sitting down for a cup of tea like a normal person, I'm immediately pulling out all the mail and sorting papers on the kitchen table. 

I just move from one thing to the next to the next, without taking a real breath. It's just go, go, go. And it's not even that I enjoy being this busy all the time, it's that I feel like I *have* to be. It's like... like if I were to just stop, if I were to just put down the trowel or leave the mail for tomorrow, the whole world would just fall apart. Or at least, I would fall apart. It's this constant, driving pressure, even when I'm right in the middle of doing something. I'll be weeding the tomatoes and already thinking about how fast I need to drive to the senior center so I'm not late, and then at the senior center I'm thinking about the church bulletins. I'm never just *doing* the thing I'm doing, I'm already rushing toward the next thing. So yes, even when I'm active, that restlessness is right there with me, pushing me along.
Have you noticed any weight loss, increased sweating, or a faster heartbeat along with this restlessness?

Weight loss? Oh, heavens, no. No, I wish I could say I've lost weight! If anything, with all the rushing around I do, you'd think I'd be thin as a rail, wouldn't you? My sister, she lost a good ten pounds last year just from taking up walking in the mornings, and here I am running myself ragged all day long and my skirts are just as tight as they were three years ago. I suppose it's because when I do finally stop moving for a minute, I tend to grab something quick from the pantry—a handful of cookies or those little cheese crackers—because I haven't taken the time to sit down for a proper meal. So no, definitely no weight loss. 

And as for sweating... well, I mean, I sweat when I'm out in the garden, certainly. Anybody would, pulling weeds in the afternoon sun. I wear one of those wide-brimmed straw hats, but it only does so much, you know? But I don't just sit around sweating for no reason, no. Not like when I went through "the change," if you know what I mean. Oh, those hot flashes were something terrible, just waking up drenched in the middle of the night, having to change the sheets... but thank the Lord that's all behind me now. So no unusual sweating, no.

And a faster heartbeat? Hmm. Let me think about that. I wouldn't say my heart races, exactly. It's more of that... that tight, winding-up feeling in my chest that I mentioned earlier. It's not like my heart is fluttering or pounding like I've just run a marathon. It's just a very tense, uncomfortable pressure, like a coiled spring. I did have my blood pressure checked at the pharmacy last month—they have one of those little machines you can sit at, you know, right by the greeting cards—and it was perfectly normal. The pharmacist, David, he's such a nice young man, he said my numbers were excellent for my age. So I don't think there's anything wrong with my heart, it's just this awful, constant need to be doing something.
Do you notice this restlessness and need to move even while you're asleep, or does it only bother you when you're awake?

While I'm asleep? Well... I suppose that's a bit hard to answer, isn't it? Because, of course, I'm asleep! But... let me think. I do know I'm a terrible sleeper. Always have been, really, but it's just so frustrating lately. 

I'll go to bed, and I'll have the sheets all tucked in just right—I'm very particular about the sheets, I can't stand it when they get all tangled up around my ankles, it drives me absolutely up the wall. I have to buy the deep-pocket fitted sheets now because my mattress has one of those pillow tops, and the regular ones just pop right off the corners in the middle of the night. So I'll get all settled, and I'll think, "Alright, time for sleep," but my mind just keeps going and going, like we talked about.

But as for the physical restlessness... well, I don't think I'm jumping out of bed and pacing the halls in my sleep, if that's what you mean. I don't wake up standing in the kitchen or anything like that. But my daughter, Sarah, she came to stay with me for a few days last Thanksgiving. Her husband was visiting his parents, and she wanted to help me cook the turkey—which was a disaster, by the way, the oven temperature was all wrong, but that's a story for another day. Anyway, we ended up sharing the big bed in the guest room because the heater in her old room was acting up, making this awful clanking noise. 

And she told me the next morning, over coffee, she said, "Mom, you thrash around like a fish out of water!" She said I was kicking the blankets off, and then pulling them back up, and rolling over, and adjusting my pillows... just all night long. She said she hardly got a wink of sleep herself, poor thing. And I suppose she's right, because I do often wake up and the bed is just a complete disaster area. The pillows are on the floor, the top sheet is twisted like a pretzel... so I must be moving around quite a bit. But I don't remember doing it. I don't wake up feeling that awful, tight need to move like I do during the day. It's more like my body just keeps going on its own while I'm out. So I guess the answer is yes, but I don't really feel it happening, if that makes any sense at all.
Does moving around or getting up and doing something help relieve that uncomfortable feeling inside you, at least for a little while?

Relieve it? Oh... oh, I wish it did. I really, truly wish it did. You would think, wouldn't you, that if you have all this... this pent-up energy and you go scrub the baseboards or weed the garden, you'd burn it off and feel better. But it doesn't work like that for me at all. It's not like letting steam out of a kettle. 

Just the other day—it was Tuesday, I think. Yes, Tuesday, because the recycling gets picked up on Wednesday morning and I was trying to get all the bins sorted out. I was feeling so terribly wound up, just having that awful tight feeling in my chest that I told you about, so I thought, well, I'll go tackle the garage. And I was out there for three hours, moving boxes, sweeping up those little dried leaves that always blow in under the door. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he has this enormous oak tree and the leaves just get absolutely everywhere, I swear I sweep them up and the very next day they're back. 

But anyway, I was moving constantly. Up and down, lifting things, carrying heavy bags to the curb. And the whole time... the whole time, that pressure inside me didn't ease up one single bit. If anything, I just felt more frantic while I was doing it! And then when I finally came inside, completely exhausted, and tried to sit down in my recliner—it's one of those nice La-Z-Boys my son bought me for Mother's Day, it has that wonderful lumbar support—I still felt exactly as restless as I did before I started sweeping. 

So no, getting up and doing things doesn't take the feeling away. It doesn't give me any relief. It just... it just comes right along with me while I'm working, pushing me to do the next thing, and the next. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter how much I move around.

Do you ever feel that restless, uncomfortable urge to move even when you're not trying to complete a task or respond to something in your environment, like when you're completely alone with nothing to do?

Oh, heavens, yes. Even when there's absolutely nothing that needs doing, and the house is completely empty. You'd think that would be the perfect time to just relax and be still, wouldn't you? But honestly, it’s almost worse when there's nothing going on! 

I’ll try to sit down with something peaceful, just... quiet things I used to really enjoy. Like sitting with a quilt pattern, for instance. I have this beautiful Double Wedding Ring pattern I’ve been trying to piece together for my niece, Emily—she got married two years ago in June, a beautiful outdoor ceremony, though it was unseasonably warm and the buttercream on the cake practically melted—but I used to be able to just sit for hours with my fabrics and my pins and be perfectly content. Or reading my Bible! I try so hard to do my daily devotionals in the morning. I have a lovely spot by the front window, and I make myself a cup of decaf, and I sit down with this beautiful large-print Bible my late husband gave me for our twenty-fifth anniversary. 

But... well, it just doesn’t stay quiet for long. It’s like I can't just *be*. Even with no chores staring me in the face and nobody asking me for anything, I’ll be sitting there trying to read a Psalm, and before I know it, I start humming to myself. Just... humming some old hymn or a tune I heard on the radio, I don't even realize I'm doing it at first. And then I start talking to myself out loud! I'll be sitting there with my Bible open, saying things like, "Now where did I put that blue thread?" or "I wonder if the mail has come yet, I should check." 

And then the humming and the talking isn't enough, so I end up getting up out of the chair altogether. I'll just start fussing with something else entirely—straightening the doilies, or rearranging the coasters on the coffee table, or picking a piece of lint off the rug. I just abandon the quilt or the book right there on the cushion. So even when I’m completely alone and trying to do something lovely and quiet, that urge just pushes me right back up on my feet to go fuss with something.

Do you ever notice yourself making the same small movements over and over again without meaning to, like rocking back and forth, tapping your fingers constantly, or shaking your leg even when you're not aware of it?

Oh, my goodness, yes. All the time. And it's so terribly embarrassing, honestly, because just like you said, I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until someone points it out or gives me a *look*. 

Take our Wednesday morning church meetings, for example. The Women's Auxiliary meets in the fellowship hall—we've been meeting down there for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since they remodeled the basement and put in those dreadful metal folding chairs that just pinch your lower back. Anyway, we'll be sitting there, and someone will be going over the budget for the upcoming spring bake sale—which is always a whole ordeal because Mary Anne insists on pricing her pecan pies entirely too high, but nobody wants to be the one to tell her—and I'll suddenly realize that I've been just... going a mile a minute without even thinking about it. 

I'll be tapping my foot against the linoleum floor, just tap-tap-tapping away, or I'll have my purse sitting in my lap—it's this nice navy blue leather one my daughter bought me at Macy's last Christmas—and I'll just be rubbing my thumb over and over the edge of it. Just rubbing the seam, back and forth, back and forth. I do it so much I'm honestly surprised I haven't worn a hole right through the leather by now! And if I'm not doing that, I'm shifting around in my chair. I'll cross my legs, and then a minute later I have to uncross them, and then I'm leaning forward, and then I'm leaning back, and adjusting my skirt... I just can't seem to stay planted. 

And the worst part is, I truly don't notice I'm doing any of this until the ladies sitting beside me—usually it's Susan and Betty, they always save me a seat near the coffee urn—until they actually stop paying attention to the meeting and start looking over at me. They give me these little sidelong glances, you know? Just these polite but very pointed looks. And then I freeze and realize I've been wiggling and tapping and rubbing my purse like a restless schoolchild for the last twenty minutes. It makes my face burn just thinking about it, but my hands and my feet just seem to have a mind of their own!
Have you ever found yourself bothered by persistent, unwanted thoughts or felt driven to do something over and over again, even if you don't really want to do it?

Unwanted thoughts? Oh... well, let me think about that for a second. Unwanted... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my mind is certainly always going a mile a minute, just like my feet, but it's not like I'm having thoughts that bother me or scare me, if that's what you mean. It's more just... a jumble of everything all at once! 

Like yesterday, for instance. I was standing in the kitchen trying to remember if I needed more flour—I like to bake my own bread, you see, the store-bought kind just has so many preservatives these days and my late husband always preferred homemade, especially my sourdough—and suddenly I'm thinking about whether the mail carrier has come yet. And then, before I can even check the window, I'm thinking about my sister Martha in Ohio. She just had her second knee replacement, poor thing, the right one this time. The left one was back in 2018 and the physical therapy just about did her in, she was calling me every night just in tears over the exercises they made her do. But anyway, those aren't unwanted thoughts, they're just... well, they just pop in and out and crowd each other out. 

And as for feeling driven to do something over and over again... no, not really. I mean, I know I just told you about rubbing my purse or tapping my foot at the Women's Auxiliary, but that's not because I feel like I *have* to do it, or like something terrible will happen if I don't. It's just my body being restless without me realizing it. I certainly don't feel forced in my head to go check the locks fifty times or wash my hands until they're raw, like you see on those medical television programs. 

Honestly, my problem is usually the exact opposite! I can't seem to do the *same* thing for very long at all, even when I want to. I'll start washing the dishes, and then I'll see a spot on the counter, and then I'm wiping the counter, and then I notice the sugar bowl is empty so I go to the pantry, and then I'm reorganizing the spice rack... so no, I definitely don't feel stuck doing one thing over and over against my will. It's more like I'm just bouncing from one chore to the next like a pinball, and I never actually finish the dishes! So, no, I wouldn't say I have those kinds of persistent thoughts or urges at all.
Do you notice this uncomfortable urge to move mostly in the evening or when you're trying to rest, like sitting or lying down?

Mostly in the evening? Or when I'm lying down? Oh... well, let me think on that. You know, I hear people talk about things like that—my friend Barbara, for instance, she's always complaining that her legs get all twitchy and jumpy the minute she gets under the covers—but for me? No, I really wouldn't say it's mostly in the evening at all. It's really just... well, it's an all-day affair! 

I mean, certainly, if I try to sit down in the evening to watch Jeopardy—I never miss Jeopardy, it's part of my daily routine, though I must say I'm still getting used to the new hosts, it's just not the same without Alex Trebek, God rest his soul, he had such a comforting, steady voice—but if I sit in my recliner at 7:30 to watch, I'll be fidgeting and wanting to get up just as much as I do at ten o'clock in the morning. And when I finally do go to bed... well, I do toss and turn a bit. I have this lovely down comforter my daughter sent me, but sometimes it's just too warm, so I kick one leg out, and then I pull it back in. But that restless feeling, that urge to just get up and do something... it doesn't wait for the sun to go down.

It's just as likely to happen right after breakfast! Like I was saying earlier about trying to read my Bible in the morning by the front window. That's right at eight o'clock in the morning, and I'm already wanting to jump out of my chair to go fiddle with the curtains or check the thermostat. So no, it's not tied to the evening or just when I'm trying to rest. It's just... whenever I'm awake, honestly! If my eyes are open, my body wants to be moving. I could be standing in line at the grocery store at high noon—oh, the lines at the Piggly Wiggly on a Tuesday, you wouldn't believe it, it's senior discount day so everybody and their brother is there with their coupons—and I'll be shifting from foot to foot, just practically vibrating, wishing the line would move. So, no, I haven't noticed it being worse at night. It's just a constant companion, morning, noon, and night.
Do you ever notice your legs or arms moving on their own while you're asleep, like twitching or jerking, even if you're not aware of it at the time?

Moving while I'm asleep? Well, my goodness, I suppose that's a bit of a trick question, isn't it? Because if I'm asleep, I wouldn't really be aware of it to tell you! But... well, let me think. I really don't think so. 

My late husband—bless his heart, he passed away five years ago this coming May, which is just so hard to believe, the time really does just fly by, doesn't it?—well, he was an incredibly light sleeper. I mean, the man would wake up if a mouse sneezed three houses down! He always used to say he was on night watch, even though he hadn't been in the service since the seventies. Anyway, if I had been kicking or jerking my arms around in my sleep, he absolutely would have told me about it. He used to complain enough just about me stealing the sheets, let alone if I'd been treating him like a punching bag!

And since he passed, well, it's just me in that big king-sized bed. I did think about downsizing to a queen or even a full, but the mattress was practically brand new and you know how terribly expensive they are these days, it's just highway robbery. So it's just me and my miniature schnauzer, Buster. He sleeps right at the foot of the bed, right on top of that down comforter I was telling you about. And Buster, well, he's a bit of a grumpy old man himself now. He's nearly eleven, so he's quite set in his ways. If I were thrashing about or kicking my legs in the middle of the night, I'm quite sure I'd end up kicking him, and he would certainly let me know with a huff or a little growl. He hates being disturbed once he's settled. 

But he sleeps soundly right through the night, and when I wake up in the morning, the blankets aren't all torn up or kicked onto the floor or anything like that. They're usually right where they were. So, no, I don't believe I have any of that twitching or jerking going on. So I'll get all settled, and I'll think, "Alright, time for sleep," but my mind just keeps going and going, like we talked about.

But as for the physical restlessness... well, I don't think I'm jumping out of bed and pacing the halls in my sleep, if that's what you mean. I don't wake up standing in the kitchen or anything like that. But my daughter, Sarah, she came to stay with me for a few days last Thanksgiving. Her husband was visiting his parents, and she wanted to help me cook the turkey—which was a disaster, by the way, the oven temperature was all wrong, but that's a story for another day. Anyway, we ended up sharing the big bed in the guest room because the heater in her old room was acting up, making this awful clanking noise. 

And she told me the next morning, over coffee, she said, "Mom, you thrash around like a fish out of water!" She said I was kicking the blankets off, and then pulling them back up, and rolling over, and adjusting my pillows... just all night long. She said she hardly got a wink of sleep herself, poor thing. And I suppose she's right, because I do often wake up and the bed is just a complete disaster area. The pillows are on the floor, the top sheet is twisted like a pretzel... so I must be moving around quite a bit. But I don't remember doing it. I don't wake up feeling that awful, tight need to move like I do during the day. It's more like my body just keeps going on its own while I'm out. So I guess the answer is yes, but I don't really feel it happening, if that makes any sense at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is relieved by movement, which is a key feature of Restless Legs Syndrome (F06.4).
doctor.question: Does moving around or getting up and doing something help relieve that uncomfortable feeling inside you, at least for a little while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if moving around relieves the restless feeling, which is a screening question for Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) or akathisia. My symptom profile does not contain information about whether movement relieves the restlessness.

patient.answer:
Relieve it? Oh... oh, I wish it did. I really, truly wish it did. You would think, wouldn't you, that if you have all this... this pent-up energy and you go scrub the baseboards or weed the garden, you'd burn it off and feel better. But it doesn't work like that for me at all. It's not like letting steam out of a kettle. 

Just the other day—it was Tuesday, I think. Yes, Tuesday, because the recycling gets picked up on Wednesday morning and I was trying to get all the bins sorted out. I was feeling so terribly wound up, just having that awful tight feeling in my chest that I told you about, so I thought, well, I'll go tackle the garage. And I was out there for three hours, moving boxes, sweeping up those little dried leaves that always blow in under the door. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he has this enormous oak tree and the leaves just get absolutely everywhere, I swear I sweep them up and the very next day they're back. 

But anyway, I was moving constantly. Up and down, lifting things, carrying heavy bags to the curb. And the whole time... the whole time, that pressure inside me didn't ease up one single bit. If anything, I just felt more frantic while I was doing it! And then when I finally came inside, completely exhausted, and tried to sit down in my recliner—it's one of those nice La-Z-Boys my son bought me for Mother's Day, it has that wonderful lumbar support—I still felt exactly as restless as I did before I started sweeping. 

So no, getting up and doing things doesn't take the feeling away. It doesn't give me any relief. It just... it just comes right along with me while I'm working, pushing me to do the next thing, and the next. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter how much I move around.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is present in the absence of external stimuli or specific tasks, to assess for akathisia or internal agitation unrelated to goal-directed activity.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that restless, uncomfortable urge to move even when you're not trying to complete a task or respond to something in your environment, like when you're completely alone with nothing to do?

target_item.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: Quiet things I used to enjoy, like sitting with a quilt pattern or reading my Bible, don’t stay quiet for long because I start humming, talking to myself, getting up, and fussing with something else.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's ability to sit still and relax when there are no tasks to complete (quiet/leisure time), which directly corresponds to difficulty engaging in quiet leisure activities.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens, yes. Even when there's absolutely nothing that needs doing, and the house is completely empty. You'd think that would be the perfect time to just relax and be still, wouldn't you? But honestly, it’s almost worse when there's nothing going on! 

I’ll try to sit down with something peaceful, just... quiet things I used to really enjoy. Like sitting with a quilt pattern, for instance. I have this beautiful Double Wedding Ring pattern I’ve been trying to piece together for my niece, Emily—she got married two years ago in June, a beautiful outdoor ceremony, though it was unseasonably warm and the buttercream on the cake practically melted—but I used to be able to just sit for hours with my fabrics and my pins and be perfectly content. Or reading my Bible! I try so hard to do my daily devotionals in the morning. I have a lovely spot by the front window, and I make myself a cup of decaf, and I sit down with this beautiful large-print Bible my late husband gave me for our twenty-fifth anniversary. 

But... well, it just doesn’t stay quiet for long. It’s like I can't just *be*. Even with no chores staring me in the face and nobody asking me for anything, I’ll be sitting there trying to read a Psalm, and before I know it, I start humming to myself. Just... humming some old hymn or a tune I heard on the radio, I don't even realize I'm doing it at first. And then I start talking to myself out loud! I'll be sitting there with my Bible open, saying things like, "Now where did I put that blue thread?" or "I wonder if the mail has come yet, I should check." 

And then the humming and the talking isn't enough, so I end up getting up out of the chair altogether. I'll just start fussing with something else entirely—straightening the doilies, or rearranging the coasters on the coffee table, or picking a piece of lint off the rug. I just abandon the quilt or the book right there on the cushion. So even when I’m completely alone and trying to do something lovely and quiet, that urge just pushes me right back up on my feet to go fuss with something.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's restlessness and need to move are accompanied by repetitive, involuntary movements or tics, which could suggest a neurological component such as akathisia or stereotypy.
doctor.question: Do you ever notice yourself making the same small movements over and over again without meaning to, like rocking back and forth, tapping your fingers constantly, or shaking your leg even when you're not aware of it?

target_item.name: Fidgeting
target_item.manifestation: Even in church meetings I am tapping my foot, rubbing the edge of my purse, or shifting around in the chair until the ladies beside me start looking over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repetitive small movements like tapping fingers or shaking a leg, which directly maps to the symptom of fidgeting.

patient.answer:
Oh, my goodness, yes. All the time. And it's so terribly embarrassing, honestly, because just like you said, I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until someone points it out or gives me a *look*. 

Take our Wednesday morning church meetings, for example. The Women's Auxiliary meets in the fellowship hall—we've been meeting down there for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since they remodeled the basement and put in those dreadful metal folding chairs that just pinch your lower back. Anyway, we'll be sitting there, and someone will be going over the budget for the upcoming spring bake sale—which is always a whole ordeal because Mary Anne insists on pricing her pecan pies entirely too high, but nobody wants to be the one to tell her—and I'll suddenly realize that I've been just... going a mile a minute without even thinking about it. 

I'll be tapping my foot against the linoleum floor, just tap-tap-tapping away, or I'll have my purse sitting in my lap—it's this nice navy blue leather one my daughter bought me at Macy's last Christmas—and I'll just be rubbing my thumb over and over the edge of it. Just rubbing the seam, back and forth, back and forth. I do it so much I'm honestly surprised I haven't worn a hole right through the leather by now! And if I'm not doing that, I'm shifting around in my chair. I'll cross my legs, and then a minute later I have to uncross them, and then I'm leaning forward, and then I'm leaning back, and adjusting my skirt... I just can't seem to stay planted. 

And the worst part is, I truly don't notice I'm doing any of this until the ladies sitting beside me—usually it's Susan and Betty, they always save me a seat near the coffee urn—until they actually stop paying attention to the meeting and start looking over at me. They give me these little sidelong glances, you know? Just these polite but very pointed looks. And then I freeze and realize I've been wiggling and tapping and rubbing my purse like a restless schoolchild for the last twenty minutes. It makes my face burn just thinking about it, but my hands and my feet just seem to have a mind of their own!

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restlessness is accompanied by intrusive, unwanted thoughts or compulsive behaviors that may indicate obsessive-compulsive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself bothered by persistent, unwanted thoughts or felt driven to do something over and over again, even if you don't really want to do it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about obsessions and compulsions (symptoms of OCD), which are not part of my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Unwanted thoughts? Oh... well, let me think about that for a second. Unwanted... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my mind is certainly always going a mile a minute, just like my feet, but it's not like I'm having thoughts that bother me or scare me, if that's what you mean. It's more just... a jumble of everything all at once! 

Like yesterday, for instance. I was standing in the kitchen trying to remember if I needed more flour—I like to bake my own bread, you see, the store-bought kind just has so many preservatives these days and my late husband always preferred homemade, especially my sourdough—and suddenly I'm thinking about whether the mail carrier has come yet. And then, before I can even check the window, I'm thinking about my sister Martha in Ohio. She just had her second knee replacement, poor thing, the right one this time. The left one was back in 2018 and the physical therapy just about did her in, she was calling me every night just in tears over the exercises they made her do. But anyway, those aren't unwanted thoughts, they're just... well, they just pop in and out and crowd each other out. 

And as for feeling driven to do something over and over again... no, not really. I mean, I know I just told you about rubbing my purse or tapping my foot at the Women's Auxiliary, but that's not because I feel like I *have* to do it, or like something terrible will happen if I don't. It's just my body being restless without me realizing it. I certainly don't feel forced in my head to go check the locks fifty times or wash my hands until they're raw, like you see on those medical television programs. 

Honestly, my problem is usually the exact opposite! I can't seem to do the *same* thing for very long at all, even when I want to. I'll start washing the dishes, and then I'll see a spot on the counter, and then I'm wiping the counter, and then I notice the sugar bowl is empty so I go to the pantry, and then I'm reorganizing the spice rack... so no, I definitely don't feel stuck doing one thing over and over against my will. It's more like I'm just bouncing from one chore to the next like a pinball, and I never actually finish the dishes! So, no, I wouldn't say I have those kinds of persistent thoughts or urges at all.

doctor.intent: Ask about the presence of a strong, uncomfortable urge to move that occurs specifically in the evening or at rest, which is a key feature of Restless Legs Syndrome (F06.4).
doctor.question: Do you notice this uncomfortable urge to move mostly in the evening or when you're trying to rest, like sitting or lying down?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms characteristic of Restless Legs Syndrome (urge to move legs worsening in the evening or at rest), which is not covered by the patient's ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Mostly in the evening? Or when I'm lying down? Oh... well, let me think on that. You know, I hear people talk about things like that—my friend Barbara, for instance, she's always complaining that her legs get all twitchy and jumpy the minute she gets under the covers—but for me? No, I really wouldn't say it's mostly in the evening at all. It's really just... well, it's an all-day affair! 

I mean, certainly, if I try to sit down in the evening to watch Jeopardy—I never miss Jeopardy, it's part of my daily routine, though I must say I'm still getting used to the new hosts, it's just not the same without Alex Trebek, God rest his soul, he had such a comforting, steady voice—but if I sit in my recliner at 7:30 to watch, I'll be fidgeting and wanting to get up just as much as I do at ten o'clock in the morning. And when I finally do go to bed... well, I do toss and turn a bit. I have this lovely down comforter my daughter sent me, but sometimes it's just too warm, so I kick one leg out, and then I pull it back in. But that restless feeling, that urge to just get up and do something... it doesn't wait for the sun to go down.

It's just as likely to happen right after breakfast! Like I was saying earlier about trying to read my Bible in the morning by the front window. That's right at eight o'clock in the morning, and I'm already wanting to jump out of my chair to go fiddle with the curtains or check the thermostat. So no, it's not tied to the evening or just when I'm trying to rest. It's just... whenever I'm awake, honestly! If my eyes are open, my body wants to be moving. I could be standing in line at the grocery store at high noon—oh, the lines at the Piggly Wiggly on a Tuesday, you wouldn't believe it, it's senior discount day so everybody and their brother is there with their coupons—and I'll be shifting from foot to foot, just practically vibrating, wishing the line would move. So, no, I haven't noticed it being worse at night. It's just a constant companion, morning, noon, and night.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is related to a psychiatric condition like anxiety or a neurological condition like restless legs syndrome by assessing if it occurs during sleep and is associated with involuntary movements.
doctor.question: Do you ever notice your legs or arms moving on their own while you're asleep, like twitching or jerking, even if you're not aware of it at the time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about involuntary limb movements during sleep (like twitching or jerking), which is a screening question for sleep-related movement disorders such as Periodic Limb Movement Disorder. This is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Moving while I'm asleep? Well, my goodness, I suppose that's a bit of a trick question, isn't it? Because if I'm asleep, I wouldn't really be aware of it to tell you! But... well, let me think. I really don't think so. 

My late husband—bless his heart, he passed away five years ago this coming May, which is just so hard to believe, the time really does just fly by, doesn't it?—well, he was an incredibly light sleeper. I mean, the man would wake up if a mouse sneezed three houses down! He always used to say he was on night watch, even though he hadn't been in the service since the seventies. Anyway, if I had been kicking or jerking my arms around in my sleep, he absolutely would have told me about it. He used to complain enough just about me stealing the sheets, let alone if I'd been treating him like a punching bag!

And since he passed, well, it's just me in that big king-sized bed. I did think about downsizing to a queen or even a full, but the mattress was practically brand new and you know how terribly expensive they are these days, it's just highway robbery. So it's just me and my miniature schnauzer, Buster. He sleeps right at the foot of the bed, right on top of that down comforter I was telling you about. And Buster, well, he's a bit of a grumpy old man himself now. He's nearly eleven, so he's quite set in his ways. If I were thrashing about or kicking my legs in the middle of the night, I'm quite sure I'd end up kicking him, and he would certainly let me know with a huff or a little growl. He hates being disturbed once he's settled. 

But he sleeps soundly right through the night, and when I wake up in the morning, the blankets aren't all torn up or kicked onto the floor or anything like that. They're usually right where they were. So, no, I don't believe I have any of that twitching or jerking going on. I mean, I toss and turn a bit when I'm *trying* to get comfortable, like I mentioned before, but once I'm actually out like a light? I think I'm pretty still. At least, as far as I know! Unless Buster is keeping secrets from me, but no, I haven't noticed anything like that at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences an urge to move that is not better explained by another medical or psychiatric condition, and to further differentiate between possible diagnoses like F90.0 (ADHD), F41.1 (GAD), and F06.4 (Restless Legs Syndrome).
doctor.question: Do you ever feel this urge to move even during routine activities that require you to stay still, like sitting in a doctor's office, watching a movie, or riding in a car for a long time?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore, like I have to jump up and do the next thing even when I am worn out and should be sitting still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the urge to move in situations where it is expected to stay still, which maps directly to feeling restless in inappropriate situations.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. That is exactly it. In fact, that's really the main reason I finally decided to come in and see you. I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's the most frustrating thing in the world, because even when I am just completely worn out to the bone, and I know I should just be sitting still and resting, I feel like I have to jump up and do the next thing. 

Like you said, riding in a car... oh, don't even get me started on long car rides! My daughter, Susan—she's the one who lives down in Atlanta now, she moved there a few years ago for her husband's job, he works in logistics, whatever that actually means—well, she drove us down to Florida last spring for a little mother-daughter getaway. It was supposed to be relaxing, just the two of us, but sitting in that passenger seat for all those hours? I thought I was going to lose my mind! I kept adjusting the air conditioning vents, and opening and closing the glove compartment, and asking if we could pull over at every single rest stop. Not because I even needed to use the facilities, mind you, but just because I had to get out and pace around the parking lot for a minute. Susan was getting so exasperated with me, she finally said, "Mom, we're never going to get to Daytona at this rate!" 

And movies? I haven't been to a proper movie theater since before the pandemic—they charge an arm and a leg for a simple bucket of popcorn anyway, it's practically a car payment—but even just sitting in the waiting room out there before your nurse called me back! I tried to sit still. I really did. There were some magazines on the little table, I think there was a Better Homes and Gardens from 2021, and I picked it up, put it down, crossed my legs, uncrossed them, tapped my fingers on my purse... I just couldn't settle. 

It doesn't matter if it's a doctor's office or my own living room. Even when my joints are aching and I am just so tired I could cry, I still get that terrible restless feeling, like my body just refuses to acknowledge that it's time to stop. It's honestly just exhausting, being this wound up all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is relieved by movement, which is a key feature in differentiating Restless Legs Syndrome from other conditions.
doctor.question: Does moving your legs or walking around help relieve that uncomfortable feeling inside you, at least for a little while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if moving the legs or walking around relieves the uncomfortable feeling, which is a screening question for Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS). This specific symptom is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Relieve it? Oh, I wish it did! You would think that getting up and walking around would burn it off, wouldn't you? That is exactly what my sister-in-law, Martha, always tells me. She says I should just walk it off, go take a turn around the garden, get some fresh air. And I do try, I really do. I will get up from my recliner, the one I was telling you about where I watch my shows, and I will pace right through the living room, down the hall, past the guest bathroom that I really need to get someone to re-caulk, and straight into the kitchen. I might wipe down the counters or go check the mail out front just to be doing something. 

But honestly? No, it really does not relieve that feeling at all. Not even for a minute! It is not like scratching an itch where you finally get some relief. It is more like I am just taking that awful, wound-up feeling on a walking tour of my house! Even while my legs are moving and I am walking around, my mind is still just buzzing, and I still feel that terrible urge to be doing something else. So I will be walking, but I am still feeling just as restless as when I was sitting down. I could walk all the way down to the Piggly Wiggly and back, and I would still feel like a coiled spring the entire time. So no, the moving does not actually make the uncomfortable feeling go away, it just means I am uncomfortable while standing up instead of uncomfortable while sitting down! It is terribly frustrating.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient's restlessness is relieved by movement, which would help differentiate Restless Legs Syndrome (F06.4) from other conditions.
doctor.question: Does moving your legs or walking around help relieve that uncomfortable feeling inside you, at least for a little while?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if moving the legs relieves the uncomfortable feeling, which is a symptom of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS). This specific symptom (relief of urge by movement) is not in the patient's ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, goodness, didn't I just... or maybe I didn't explain it quite right just now. Like I was saying about pacing down the hall, no, it really doesn't give me any relief at all. I know you just asked that, so maybe you meant something slightly different? But no, walking around doesn't settle me down. 

It's just like I was telling you, that uncomfortable feeling just follows me right into the kitchen or out to the mailbox. I suppose... well, I suppose people think if you move, you're burning off whatever is making you restless. But for me, it's like the motor is still running on high no matter what my legs are doing. And at my age, let me tell you, just walking around for the sake of it isn't exactly a treat anyway! I've had terrible trouble with my arches since my mid-forties—I have to buy those special orthotic inserts, the ones they sell over at the pharmacy on Main Street, they cost a small fortune—so I really only want to be on my feet if I have a good reason to be. 

But when I get that awful wound-up feeling, I end up on my feet anyway, pacing around, and it doesn't do a lick of good. I just end up with sore feet on top of feeling like I want to jump out of my own skin. So, no, moving doesn't help relieve it one bit, even for a second.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a persistent, pervasive sense of restlessness and an almost constant need to be moving, primarily involving the entire body rather than just the legs. This is not secondary to anxiety, depression, or a mood episode, and is not better explained by another condition such as hyperthyroidism or a movement disorder. The presentation is most consistent with Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) in the context of late-onset ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation, which is recognized under F90.0 in ICD-10. The chronic, lifelong pattern of motor restlessness, inability to remain still even when desired, and associated functional impairment aligns with this diagnosis.
